title: Sudip Nag | Ian Millner - Capital A

sentences.text: Hello.
Hi.
How you doing?
Very relaxed.
I'm all right.
Well, it's, uh, it's gin and tonic o'clock, isn't it?
Over here.
So I should be.
Yes.
Because you've been hanging out with those Koreans.
Th arch, I think.
Well, best, best say nothing about that.
We've got like a month of auditing at the moment, so.
I have you.
Yeah.
Well, good to see you anyway.
Looking well.
Suede.
Nice to see you too.
Same here indeed.
Very nice to meet you.
How you doing?
Good, how are you?
Ian.
Nice to meet you too.
Yeah, not bad, thank you.
I noticed you went to school.
Liverpool.
My favorite team, so.
Oh, that's, this is great news.
We could spend the whole call talking about that.
Right?
From my childhood though, right?
In Russian.
Kennedy at least, so, yeah.
Oh yeah, fantastic.
That was a long time ago.
Yeah, sorry.
Go and see that.
Yeah, sorry.
I'm ready for you to go.
I will just give it.
Oh, sure.
I'm sure you both know enough about each other.
But anyway, obviously it's much my pleasure to introduce Ian.
Ian's company does work as a client as well on a current search in the US, but this isn't part of our mandate at all, looking for companies like yours.
But Ian's company, Iris, is a fantastic match for what it is that you've been proposing.
And normally working on acquisitions obviously, is what we normally do.
So the idea of a JV is obviously a little bit left field, but I'll give you the floor and see if there's some chemistry and some commonalities that are worth exploring more.
Sounds great.
Ian, would it help if you gave me overview of what you guys do so I can see how it fits within the context of what you do.
You want to know about Iris?
Yeah.
Yeah, yeah.
Okay, so we're 25 years old, we're now part of the Samsung group.
We've got offices all over the world, just under 1000 people.
We're a creative company, so we're advertising, content, pr, digital, search, CRM.
So our go to market is all about participation and helping clients navigate a world where earned and owned.
Our leading paid so.
And our biggest clients, funnily enough, is Samsung.
But we also work with Adidas, Barclays, Pizza Hut, a range of other clients all over the world.
And I founded the company, oversaw its growth for 25 years or so, and now I'm the chair of the business.
I've also been working for our parent company, helping them make sense of all their agencies and all of their clients too.
And the last year and a half.
I've basically been engaged in a transformation project to refocus the business, make sure it's future ready, hire a load of amazing people and exit one or two people as well.
So I've been doing quite a lot of, I've had a good transfer window I think, the last few months.
And just one last other thing.
In addition to that, I also work as a non exec chair for a couple of other businesses too.
So I've been doing all sorts of things, but fundamentally I'm an entrepreneur in the creative industries.
Lovely, I think.
Yeah, so that's great.
So VR.
So what kind of.
First, let me ask you a few questions.
What kind of markets are you guys focused on?
Like, obviously it's consumer more mainly, I would imagine, but like apparel, food and what kind of verticals are you in?

So a range, so lots of healthcare, pharmaceutical, obviously consumer goods, consumer electronics, a lot of b, two b, a lot of tech, a lot of financial services, a lot of quick service, restaurants, hotels, leisure, government, what else?
I mean, honestly pretty active in most of, in most categories, either currently or previously.
So it's a really good range.
And obviously the exact mix varies a bit by the office we're talking about.
And you talked about helping on the creative side, mainly with customers.
Do you also help with innovation or is it mainly creatives?
So I would say that good creative is innovation.
So our company isn't traditional advertising agency.
Okay, perfect.
Our company is all about finding ideas for problems.
Perfect.
And so they're less.
The way we look at the world is more about creative innovation.
In fact, we used to describe ourselves as a creative innovation network.
Perfect.
So we are, we are a little bit different from what you do.
We are a company that helps understand what consumers want, how they behave and what are the emotional and functional triggers of choice for consumers in a particular market.
And using that information, we help our customers understand how the market segments from an experience perspective.

What experiences are consumer looking for, customer looking for in a particular market and what the drivers of those experiences are, what the, where the brands fit in that particular context of that market.
And therefore how can the brands be positioned to one application repositioning or brand positioning with regards to what customers looking for and what, how they perceive your brand today.
Not just perceive but behave against your brand, like why they buy your brand today.
And that gives you clues into how can we position to capture higher share.
So it being the science behind the creative, we're not the creative ones.
We actually hand off to someone like your agency to then build the creative.
So we bring a lot of consumer science, data science and AI to the problem, to be able to sift out of what really matters and what remove the needle.
So things like market maps, like brand competition, who do you actually compete with and on what attributes and how to reposition the brand?
First of all, like I mentioned, so feed, feed into creatives.
The third thing is how to target customers or consumers, what targets to go after, what media to go after because of that, because your information on media as well as to the customer set.
And the reason I offer innovation is also understand what function attributes customers are looking for in the context of the experiences, and therefore be able to drive products as well.
How do the product actually satisfy the needs, both the emotional and functional needs?
And what are the gaps, therefore, and how do you go fill the gaps?
So that's kind of typically you would do, but we're bringing a lot of science to the problem.
And who would you, who would you say you compete with most often?
We compete with McKenzie, Bain and BCG mainly.
Mainly.
And I was ministering to Andy, therefore we had acquisition offers from them, all three.
But we choose to be independent.
We think we can scale a lot more and we think we are better off pairing with someone like yourself because you are not doing the same things we are doing.
But you're expanding the value chain, if you will.
Yeah.
And do you remember what if?
Yeah.
The what if part are you talking about?
Yes, because.
Because it's a model, remember?
So we can do simulations to do what ifs.
Yes, absolutely.
We quantify everything.

And so you can say that a particular driver, if you say juicy in a drink, juicy, or let's say robustness, quote unquote, for a coffee, we can tell you how important that driver is, was another driver in terms of quant, which means this is, let's say the highest driver is 100%.
I can tell you the next driver is 80% influence on choice.
So you can say what's really important was not important.
So we bring in the math and quantification to both emotions and functions, functional attributes.
I got you.
So that's what we're doing.

And I was wondering what your thoughts are in terms of how this may or may not jive with what you do today and what you might need in terms of making your creatives more robust and more, I would say, growth oriented for the, for the customer.
Yeah.
So, I mean, it's a brilliant.
What you described is brilliant and really interesting.
I think this will boil down to chemistry.
It'll be about how do we get on?
Do we like each other?
Can we work together?
It'll be one of those, I think, because the skills and the, the process you're describing is fantastic.

And so I think the best thing for us to do would be to just get your main people and our main people together at a point in time, either probably initially over Zoom or it can be physical, depending on where you've got folks, and talk about it.
Because I know that we just got a couple of new creative leaders and they're super smart, very ambitious.
They're looking to make a difference.
They want to be revolutionary with their work.
So I think partnering could easily unlock some opportunities in that.
Lovely.
I think that's the best way to do this in some sense of you get a feel for what we do and how we do things.
If you get a feel for how you do things, and that'll really help.
Yeah, I think so.
So, yeah, sorry.
Yeah, let's do that.
Let's do that.
So, Andy, have any thoughts?
Yeah.
Excuse me.
I choked as soon as I spoke.
Sorry.
Do you need a drink of water?
Yeah, probably.
It's so late.
I should be in bed.
Yeah.
So all I was going to suggest was that we get some times from both sides and set them, set up something that's really going to work.
Sudip, what sort, sort of the size of your team that would be able to interface with Ian's team.
I think really what we would need is from our side with two main people.
I think that should be enough for someone who understands the data side and the analytic side and myself.
So I think a couple of people on our side should be enough to dive the discussion.
That's what we've done in the past with like McKenzie and BCG and so on.
So I think that keeps the team small, more focused for us from our perspective.
Okay.
Sorry.
What time zones are they in?
Myself and my partners, both in the, in the Pacific time zone.
Right.
Okay.
We're in San Francisco.
Yeah.
And for you, Ian, what, what would you need?
What would your team need?
Do they need a presentation or is it just a conversation?
What's your preference?
I think conversation would be good.
I think let's start with the conversation.
So we get a high level understanding and connection there and then take it from there to what we focus on.

I think the end goal, the way I was thinking about it, guys, is the proof will be in the pudding in terms of doing a pilot project together and kind of put resource from our side, resource from your side and see how that goes and fine tune that to make that a blueprint for ongoing work, if that works out.
Yeah.
There'll be a brief bit of show and tell so that we understand the quality of each other's work and our perspectives and.
Absolutely.
And then I think we'll create some sort of agenda.
I think we can work on it together ahead of the meeting just to sort of guide the discussion to see if there's a sort of meeting of minds.
I think we'll have a couple of the key creative guys and they're both us based, maybe the us based CEO and then maybe one guy from London.
So there might be like four or five people from us, but most of them will be us based.
Perfect.
That'd be fine.
And we can show you some things that you've done so you get a feel for actual output.
Yeah, yeah.
All right.
That sounds good.
Perfect.
So where do we go from here?
Andy, will you be helping us put together?
Yeah, of course.
Yeah.

I'll get that set up because I've got everybody's contact details, so I'm sure Ian will put me in touch with somebody on his team and we'll look at their availability and get something set up for you, Sudip, so we can go through that.
Yeah, probably next couple of weeks would be good.
Before it gets too quick.
Is that going to work for you?
I don't think so.
It'll be, we've got a massive pitch on in Dallas, so.
And everybody that I've just talked about is involved in that in one way shape or so.
This will just be an unwelcome distraction.
So it'll probably be less.
Where are we now?
Just before November, aren't we?
So, yeah, so it'll be like, it'll be like third week in November, I think.
But if we, if we just knock about some options, you know, I can, I can make sure we, you know, have a proper slot that won't get derailed by the, uh, people getting busy.
Okay.
All right.
So I'll set that up.
Suit it.
No, no worries about that.
Um, and we'll get a slot in, and in the meantime, we'll get some preparation together with an agenda that suits CN's team what we can present.
Perfect.
All right, brilliant.
Thank you very much for your time, Ian.
Thanks so much again.
Nice to meet you.
Nice to meet you.
I'll see you soon.
Take care.
Bye bye bye.
Have a good evening.
Cheers.

summary.overview: In the Introductory Business Meeting between Sudip Nag and Ian Millner, key representatives from Sudip's company and Ian's company, Iris, discussed potential partnership opportunities centered around a Joint Venture (JV) instead of an acquisition. Following introductions, Ian provided an overview of Iris—a creative agency with 25 years of experience and a global presence, serving major clients like Samsung and Adidas—while Sudip explained his firm's focus on consumer behavior analysis and market insights. Both parties expressed mutual interest in collaboration, highlighting the importance of team chemistry, and proposed a meeting between key personnel to explore synergies. Plans were made for a follow-up meeting in the third week of November, with Andy Day coordinating logistics and preparing an agenda, while both Sudip and Ian committed to creating presentation materials for the discussions.
summary.short_summary: In a recent introductory meeting, Sudip Nag and Ian Millner explored opportunities for collaboration between their companies through a Joint Venture (JV) instead of an acquisition. Ian presented Iris, a creative agency with 25 years of experience and a global presence, highlighting their major clients like Samsung and Adidas, while Sudip shared insights about his firm’s focus on consumer behavior analysis and market insights. Both parties agreed on the importance of team chemistry and proposed a follow-up meeting to discuss potential synergies, with Andy Day coordinating logistics and preparing an agenda. Plans were made for a meeting in the third week of November, during which Sudip and Ian committed to developing presentation materials to facilitate discussions.
